content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) published guidelines in 2006 for hand hygiene practices in intensive care units (ICUs), emphasizing the importance of proper hand hygiene to prevent healthcare-associated infections (HAIs). Fitzpatrick et al. (2009) highlighted the role of cultural change in improving hand hygiene compliance, stating that clean hands save lives. Grayson et al. (2008) demonstrated significant reductions in methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) bacteremia through a multisite hand hygiene culture-change program, which was later successfully implemented statewide. Hawn et al. (2011) argued for advancements in surgical site infection (SSI) prevention beyond the Surgical Care Improvement Program, emphasizing the need for innovative strategies. Hong et al. (2013) reported a decrease in central-line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSIs) in Connecticut ICUs through collaborative quality improvement efforts. Hsu et al. (2014) examined the impact of self-reported compliance with infection prevention guidelines, finding a correlation with reduced bloodstream infections in a national collaborative. Lin et al. (2012) described the successful eradication of CLABSIs in Hawaii through a statewide initiative. Mehta et al. (2013) demonstrated the effectiveness of a multidimensional approach in preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) across 21 ICUs in India, as part of the International Nosocomial Infection Control Consortium (INICC). Patel et al. (2013) reported reduced bloodstream infection rates in outpatient hemodialysis facilities participating in a collaborative prevention effort. Pronovost et al. (2006, 2010) described interventions to reduce catheter-related bloodstream infections (CRBSIs) in ICUs, including the Keystone ICU Project, which achieved sustained reductions in Michigan ICUs. Roberts et al. (2012) detailed the implementation and sustainability of a hand hygiene culture-change program at Auckland District Health Board. Rosenthal et al. (2012) demonstrated the effectiveness of a multidimensional strategy in reducing VAP in pediatric ICUs across five developing countries. Rosenthal et al. (2012) also reported on the success of a similar approach in adult ICUs across 14 developing countries, spanning four continents. Sinuff et al. (2013) evaluated the implementation of clinical practice guidelines for VAP prevention in a multicenter prospective study. Stone et al. (2012) assessed the impact of the Clean Your Hands campaign in England and Wales, which led to reductions in MRSA bacteremia and Clostridium difficile infections. Toltzis et al. (2014) described a statewide collaborative to reduce pediatric SSIs, while Wirtzchafer et al. (2010) reported on a similar initiative to reduce neonatal CLABSIs. Warren et al. (2006) demonstrated the success of a multicenter intervention in preventing CLABSIs. Weeks et al. (2014) highlighted the influence of a multifaceted intervention on central line days in ICUs. Pantle et al. (2009) described a statewide approach to systematizing hand hygiene behavior in hospitals. Berenholtz et al. (2011) reported on a collaborative cohort study to reduce VAP in ICUs. Fisher et al. (2013) detailed efforts to reduce CLABSIs in North Carolina neonatal ICUs. Ben-David et al. (2014) described a national intervention in Israel to prevent the spread of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae in post-acute care hospitals. Bone et al. (2008) reported on a quality improvement collaborative in Veterans Affairs hospitals, which reduced VAP and CRBSI rates. Evans et al. (2013) described the Veterans Affairs MRSA prevention initiative, which achieved sustained reductions in MRSA transmission and HAIs. Koll et al. (2014) detailed a collaborative intervention model to prevent hospital-onset Clostridium difficile infections in the New York metropolitan region. Kralovic et al. (2013) highlighted the success of the Veterans Affairs MRSA Prevention Initiative in achieving zero MRSA infections. Morris et al. (2015) described early progress in a new SSI improvement program in New Zealand. Muto et al. (2005) reported reductions in CLABSIs among ICU patients. Saint et al. (2013) examined efforts to prevent catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) in the United States. Stulberg et al. (2010) analyzed adherence to surgical care improvement project measures and their association with postoperative infections. Unahalekhaka et al. (2007) described a collaborative effort to reduce VAP in Thailand. Dixon-Woods et al. (2013) conducted an ethnographic study of the Matching Michigan patient safety program. Render et al. (2011) reported on the reduction of central line infections in Veterans Administration ICUs through a central infrastructure supporting learning and improvement. Herzer et al. (2014) evaluated the cost-effectiveness of a quality improvement program to reduce CLABSIs in U.S. ICUs. Slayton et al. (2015) analyzed the cost-benefit of federal investment in preventing Clostridium difficile infections through multifaceted infection control and antimicrobial stewardship programs. The National Institute for Clinical Excellence (2002) outlined principles for best practices in clinical audit. Charrier et al. (2008) demonstrated the use of integrated audits to implement unit protocols in a randomized controlled study. Moongtui et al. (2000) reported on the use of peer feedback to improve handwashing and glove usage among Thai healthcare workers. Yinnon et al. (2012) described the use of report cards to improve infection control guideline implementation and reduce nosocomial infection rates. Cocanour et al. (2006) reported on efforts to decrease VAP in a trauma ICU. Kilbride et al. (2003) described the implementation of evidence-based practices to reduce nosocomial infections. Armellino et al. (2013) demonstrated the replication of hand hygiene improvements in a surgical ICU using remote video auditing and feedback. McGuckin et al. (2009) reported on hand hygiene compliance rates in the United States through a multicenter collaboration. The World Health Organization (2016) provided a user manual for workload indicators of staffing need (WISN). Alonso-Echanove et al. (2003) examined the effect of nurse staffing and antimicrobial-impregnated central venous catheters on bloodstream infection risk in ICUs. Blatnik and Lesnicar (2006) reported on the propagation of MRSA due to nurse overloading in ICUs. Borg (2003) analyzed the impact of bed occupancy and overcrowding on MRSA infection incidence in general wards. Cunningham et al. (2006) examined the relationship between bed occupancy, turnover intervals, and MRSA rates in English hospitals. Howie and Ridley (2008) reported on the association between bed occupancy and MRSA infection incidence in an ICU. Hugonnet et al. (2007) analyzed the effect of workload on infection risk in critically ill patients. Hugonnet et al. (2007) also identified staffing levels as a determinant of late-onset VAP. Hugonnet et al. (2007) further evaluated the relationship between nurse staffing levels and nosocomial infections using case-crossover and case-time-control designs. Mark et al. (2007) examined the impact of nurse staffing on adverse events in hospitalized children. Nijssen et al. (2003) assessed the relative risk of pathogen transmission by physicians and nurses in a medical ICU. Vicca (1999) identified nursing staff workload as a determinant of MRSA spread in an adult intensive therapy unit. Fridkin et al. (1996) highlighted the role of understaffing in central venous catheter-associated bloodstream infections. Petrosillo et al. (2001) reported on the role of understaffing in hepatitis C virus transmission in dialysis settings. Robert et al. (2000) analyzed the influence of nursing staff composition on primary bloodstream infection rates in a surgical ICU. Borg et al. (2003) conducted a time-series analysis of the impact of bed occupancy rates on infection rates.
